name: St. Raymond Nonnatus
title: Mercedarian friar, ransomer of captives
summary: Raymond Nonnatus was a 13th-century Mercedarian friar from Catalonia, whose order ransomed Christians held captive in North Africa. Tradition says he stayed behind as a hostage when the money ran out, though little of his story can be checked. Patron of childbirth, expectant mothers and captives, he is a saint the monks can ask to stand by the Prep's young families.
life: Raymond was born around 1204 in Catalonia, in northeastern Spain, traditionally at Portell. His surname is a nickname. Non natus means "not born", and the story behind it is that his mother died in labor and he was cut from her womb. That story is the reason he became the patron of childbirth, of midwives and of mothers expecting a child.

As a young man he joined the Order of Our Lady of Mercy, the Mercedarians, founded at Barcelona around 1218 by St. Peter Nolasco. The order existed for one work. In those years Christians taken at sea or on the coasts of Spain were held for ransom in North Africa, and many were never freed. The Mercedarians collected money, crossed to Algiers and Tunis, and bought them back. Its friars took a fourth vow, beyond poverty, chastity and obedience, to give themselves as hostages if that was the only way to free a captive in danger of losing his faith.

The tradition of the order says that Raymond did exactly that. When the ransom money ran out, he stayed behind in place of others. In captivity he kept preaching and baptized some of his guards, and his captors are said to have pierced his lips with a hot iron and closed his mouth with a padlock. After some months the order paid his ransom and he came home.

The story goes on to say that Pope Gregory IX named him a cardinal and that he died at Cardona, near Barcelona, in 1240, on his way to Rome, still dressed as a poor friar. Most of this comes from the Mercedarians' own later tradition, and very little of it can be checked against records of the time. He was never canonized by a formal process, but his cult was approved and his name was entered in the Roman Martyrology in the 17th century. His feast was taken off the General Roman Calendar in 1969, and it is still kept by his order and in many places.
why_here: A school is full of families, and families are always beginning. Teachers and staff at the Prep, parents of students, and alumni marry and have children. Raymond is the saint people have long asked to stand by a mother in labor and by a child just born, and the monks can pray to him for those families by name.

His order also keeps alive a hard idea that fits the monastery. A Mercedarian promised to take another person's place if it came to that. Monks promise obedience and stability, which means staying and serving where they are put, often for the sake of people they will never meet. Whatever the details of Raymond's own story, that is the life he stands for.
relic: One relic in the oval of royal saints and the House of Este in an ornate gold frame, labelled "S. Raim. Non." ("Raym. Non." in another view).
check: His birthplace (Portell) and the cardinalate are tradition, not record. The year his name entered the Roman Martyrology (often given as 1657) is not stated here and could be verified.

name: St. Remigius
title: Bishop of Reims, who baptized Clovis
feast: 1 October (13 January in the Roman Martyrology)
summary: Remigius was bishop of Reims for some seventy years, chosen at about twenty-two while still a layman. Around 500 he baptized Clovis, king of the Franks, and with him the Franks became a Catholic people. Patron of Reims and France, he suits Prep students handed responsibility early, and Benedictine monks kept his tomb at Saint-Remi for centuries.
life: Remigius, in French Rémi, was born around 437 in the north of Gaul, near Laon, into a Gallo-Roman family of some standing. The Roman Empire in the West was coming apart. Frankish, Gothic and Burgundian kings were dividing Gaul among themselves, and most of the Germanic rulers who were Christian at all were Arians, who denied that Christ is fully God.

He was still a layman, and only about twenty-two years old, when the people and clergy of Reims chose him as their bishop. He held the office for some seventy years, one of the longest episcopates on record. Little of his own writing survives, a few letters only, and much of what is told about his miracles comes from a life written centuries later by Archbishop Hincmar of Reims.

His great moment was the baptism of Clovis, king of the Franks. Clovis had married Clotilde, a Catholic princess from Burgundy, and she urged him toward the faith. Around the year 500 (historians still argue over the exact year, anywhere from 496 to about 508) Remigius baptized him at Reims at Christmas, together with some three thousand of his warriors. Gregory of Tours, writing about seventy years later, gives the bishop's words at the font. "Bow your head, proud Sicambrian. Worship what you have burned, and burn what you have worshipped." Because Clovis became Catholic and not Arian, the Franks became a Catholic people, and much of the later history of Europe followed from that.

Hincmar added the legend of the Holy Ampulla, a flask of oil said to have been brought from heaven by a dove for the baptism. The kings of France were anointed with it at Reims for centuries. That is legend, not history.

Remigius died around 533 and was buried at Reims. A Benedictine abbey, Saint-Remi, grew up around his tomb and kept it for more than a thousand years. His traditional feast, 1 October, marks the moving of his relics in 1049. The Roman Martyrology now remembers him on 13 January, the day of his death.
why_here: Remigius was made a bishop at about the age of a college senior, and he did not grow into the job by being older than everyone else. He grew into it by staying faithful for seventy years. Students at the Prep are told they will lead families, parishes and businesses sooner than they think. He is a good saint for a young person handed real responsibility early.

He also belongs to the monks in a quiet way. For most of the last thousand years his tomb was kept by Benedictine monks at Saint-Remi in Reims, who sang the office beside it as the monks of St. Bernard sing it in Cullman.
relic: One relic in the large oval of about ten relics in the velvet case studded with silver beads, labelled "S. Remigii Ep."
check: The year of Clovis's baptism is disputed (496, 498/499 and c. 508 are all argued). The number of warriors baptized with him (about 3,000) is Gregory of Tours' figure.

name: St. Roch
title: Pilgrim and nurse of the plague-stricken
summary: Roch is one of the best-loved saints of the late Middle Ages, though his life survives only in accounts written a century or more after him. The story says he nursed plague victims in Italy, caught the plague himself, and was fed by a dog. Patron against plague and of invalids, he recalls the abbey's own monks who nursed the sick in 1878 and 1918.
life: Roch, in Italian Rocco and in French Roch, is one of the most loved saints of the late Middle Ages, and one of the hardest to pin down. The oldest accounts of his life were written more than a century after he died, the earliest about 1430 and a fuller one by the Venetian Francesco Diedo in 1478. Historians do not agree even on his century, and some place his death around 1327, others around 1379.

The story says he was born at Montpellier in southern France to a wealthy family, and that he was marked from birth with a red cross on his chest. When his parents died he gave away his fortune and set out on pilgrimage to Rome. On the way he came to towns in Italy where the plague was raging. Instead of passing through, he stayed and nursed the sick in the hospitals, and many were said to be cured when he made the sign of the cross over them.

At Piacenza he caught the plague himself. Not wanting to burden anyone, he dragged himself into the woods to die. There a dog from a nearby house began to bring him bread each day, and its master, following the dog, found him and cared for him until he recovered. That is why Roch is always painted with a dog, a pilgrim's staff, and a sore on his leg.

On his way home he was arrested as a spy, during a war, and put in prison. He did not say who he was, and he died there some years later. Only after his death, the story says, was he recognized by the cross on his chest. Some recent scholars think he actually died in Lombardy, at Voghera, rather than in France.

What is certain is that his cult spread fast during the plagues of the 15th century. In 1485 his relics were brought to Venice, where the Scuola Grande di San Rocco, decorated by Tintoretto, still honors him. Wherever an epidemic struck, people built chapels to St. Roch.
why_here: St. Bernard Abbey has its own history of monks who did what the story says Roch did. In the yellow fever of 1878, Abbot Benedict Menges nursed the sick. In the flu of 1918, Frater Hubert Carney, a young monk, died nursing others. The abbey remembers both, and Roch is the saint for that kind of courage, staying with the sick when leaving would be safer.

His prayers belong as well to the monastery's infirmary, where old and sick monks are cared for by their brothers, and to a boarding school, where an illness can go through a dormitory in days. Whenever sickness comes to the hill, the monks have a patron who knew it from both sides, as nurse and as patient.
relic: One relic in the medallion in the velvet case studded with silver beads, with Sts. Francis, Anthony, Lucy and Agatha, labelled "s. Rochi Conf."
check: His dates are uncertain (deaths around 1327 and around 1379 are both proposed). The place of his death (Montpellier or Voghera) is disputed.

name: St. Sebastian
title: Roman martyr
summary: Sebastian was a real martyr of Rome, buried in the catacombs on the Appian Way, though his story comes from a later legend. It makes him a soldier shot with arrows who survived and was then beaten to death. Patron of soldiers, athletes and the sick in time of plague, he suits the Prep's athletes and coaches and the abbey's wartime chaplains.
life: Sebastian is certainly a real martyr of Rome. The oldest Roman calendar of martyrs, from the year 354, lists him on 20 January and places his burial "in the catacombs" on the Appian Way. A church was built over his tomb in the 4th century, and the catacomb and the basilica there still bear his name. St. Ambrose of Milan, writing later in that century, mentions him as a martyr who came from Milan.

Nearly everything else comes from a Passion of Sebastian written in the 5th century, a long, devout story with little claim to be history. It says he was an officer of the Praetorian Guard under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, who kept his faith quiet so that he could encourage Christians in prison. When he was found out, the emperor had him tied to a post and shot with arrows by archers of his own guard, and he was left for dead.

A widow named Irene came at night to bury him and found him still alive. She took him home and nursed him back to health. Instead of hiding or fleeing, Sebastian went and stood on the steps where the emperor would pass and rebuked him for his cruelty to Christians. This time he was beaten to death with clubs, and his body was thrown into the great sewer of Rome. A Christian woman, warned in a dream, recovered it and buried it near the catacombs.

The arrows made his name. In the ancient world plague was pictured as arrows shot from heaven, and a saint who had survived arrows seemed the right one to pray to against it. Paul the Deacon tells that when a plague struck Rome in 680, it ended after an altar was dedicated to St. Sebastian. Through the Middle Ages and the Renaissance he was painted again and again, usually as a young man bound to a post and pierced with arrows.
Because of the story he is also the patron of soldiers, archers and athletes, the last because of the strength and endurance the legend gives him.
why_here: The Prep's students include many athletes, and monks coach them and teach PE. Sebastian is the traditional patron of athletes, and he is a fitting one for a Catholic school. The legend admires his strength, but what it really praises is that he got up again and went back to finish what he had started.

He is also a soldier's saint. Monks of St. Bernard served as military chaplains in both world wars and in Korea, and some Prep graduates go on to serve. The monks can ask Sebastian to keep them, and to keep the chaplains who serve them now.
relic: One relic in a small sunburst, one of a matching pair with St. Lawrence, labelled "S. Sebastiani M."
check: His patronage of athletes is traditional, not declared by a pope. The tradition that he was a native of Milan comes from St. Ambrose.

name: St. Secundus
title: Martyr (which one is not known)
summary: The label says only "St. Secundus, martyr", and several early martyrs had that name, so which one is meant is not known. The best known is St. Secundus of Asti, patron of that city, but this is most likely a martyr from the Roman catacombs. He is a fitting companion for monks who pray daily for their own dead brothers.
life: The label on this relic says only "S. Secundi M.", "of St. Secundus, martyr". Several early martyrs had this name. The best known is St. Secundus of Asti, in Piedmont, whose legend makes him a Roman officer converted by the martyrs of his time and beheaded around 119 under the emperor Hadrian. He is the patron saint of Asti, which keeps his feast on 30 March and holds a great festival in his honor. Others named Secundus were martyred in Roman Africa and elsewhere in Italy, and a St. Secundus of Ventimiglia is counted by legend among the soldiers of the Theban Legion.

The name itself is Latin for "second", and it was common. Like the St. Agapitus whose relic shares the same small wooden box, this Secundus was most likely a martyr from the Roman catacombs, whose relics were given out from Rome in the 1700s and 1800s with handwritten labels on silk, as these are. The relic's authentication papers, if the abbey still has them, would say which Secundus is meant. Without them it is honest to say we do not know.
why_here: A martyr whose life is lost still gave it. Many of the catacomb martyrs are known now by nothing more than a name scratched near a grave, and the Church honors them anyway. The monks keep a cemetery of their own on the hill, and pray each day for brothers who have died, some long enough ago that few now living remember their faces. St. Secundus is a good companion for that work of remembering, since in his case only God keeps the rest of the story.
relic: One relic in a wooden box with a glass front, beside St. Agapitus and, most likely, St. Justina, labelled "S. Secundi M."
check: Which St. Secundus is meant. The relic's authentica, if they survive, would settle it.

name: St. Simon Stock
title: Carmelite friar and prior general
summary: Simon Stock was an English Carmelite and prior general who helped an order of hermits from Mount Carmel become an order of friars in Europe. Carmelite tradition, first written down long after his death, says Our Lady gave him the brown scapular. Patron of those who wear the scapular and of the Carmelites, he belongs with the Marian devotion of the Ave Maria Grotto.
life: Simon Stock was an Englishman, and almost nothing is known about his early life. A later legend says he went off as a boy to live as a hermit in the hollow trunk of a tree, and that this is where the name "Stock" came from. That may be a story built on the name.

He lived in the years when the Carmelites came to Europe. The order began around 1200 among hermits on Mount Carmel in the Holy Land, who lived in caves near the spring of Elijah under a short rule given by the Latin patriarch of Jerusalem. As the crusader states fell, the hermits left for Cyprus, Sicily, France and England. In the West there was little room for hermits, and the order slowly changed into an order of friars, living in towns, studying at the universities and preaching, like the Franciscans and Dominicans. It was a hard and divisive change. Simon was prior general, the head of the whole order, during part of those years, and tradition gives him much of the credit for steering the Carmelites through it.

The best-known story about him is the vision of the scapular. Carmelite tradition says that on 16 July 1251, at Cambridge, Our Lady appeared to him holding the brown scapular of the order and promised that whoever died wearing it would be saved. The story is first found in Carmelite writings from around 1400, some one hundred fifty years after his death, and many historians doubt it. The Church has never rested anything on the vision itself, but it approves the brown scapular as a sign of belonging to Mary and of a life given to her, and many Catholics wear it.

Simon died at Bordeaux on 16 May 1265, while visiting the houses of his order. He was never formally canonized, but the Carmelites have long honored him as a saint. Since 1951 part of his skull has been kept at the Carmelite friary of Aylesford in Kent.
patronage: those who wear the brown scapular
why_here: The Ave Maria Grotto, the work of Br. Joseph Zoettl, is one long act of devotion to Our Lady, and the abbey's name for it says so. St. Simon Stock is the saint most tied to the brown scapular, one of the oldest small signs of belonging to Mary, and the monks can pray to him for the pilgrims who come to the Grotto.

His life also fits the abbey's history. He helped an order of hermits from the East take root in a new country and learn a new way of living there. The monks of St. Bernard came from Bavaria to Pennsylvania and then to Alabama, and kept the Rule while learning a new land.
relic: One small theca on the large board covered in grey linen, labelled "S. Sim. Stock. C[onf.]"
check: The 1951 transfer of his skull from Bordeaux to Aylesford, and the c. 1400 date of the earliest scapular account, are from general knowledge and could be checked.

name: St. Teresa of Ávila
title: Carmelite reformer and Doctor of the Church
summary: Teresa of Ávila was a Spanish Carmelite nun who reformed her order, founded seventeen convents, and wrote The Interior Castle and other classics on prayer. In 1970 she became the first woman named a Doctor of the Church. Patron of Spain and of people in religious life, she is a practical guide for students learning to pray for themselves.
life: Teresa de Ahumada was born at Ávila in Castile on 28 March 1515. Her grandfather was a Jewish convert who had been made to do public penance by the Inquisition, a fact the family kept quiet. As a girl she read romances of chivalry and lives of the saints, and once set off with her brother to be martyred among the Moors. An uncle brought them back. In 1535, at about twenty, she entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation in Ávila.

The Incarnation was large and comfortable, with many visitors, and for almost twenty years Teresa lived an ordinary, divided life there. She was often ill, and she later wrote that for long stretches she nearly gave up prayer. Around 1554, praying before an image of the wounded Christ, she was changed. Deep experiences of prayer followed, which confessors at first suspected and later trusted.

In 1562 she founded the small, poor convent of St. Joseph in Ávila, where a few nuns would keep the Carmelite rule strictly, in enclosure, silence and poverty. It caused an uproar in the town. For the rest of her life she travelled the roads of Spain in rough carts, founding seventeen convents of the reform in all, and with St. John of the Cross she brought the reform to the friars. She met opposition from her own order, from officials and from the Inquisition, which examined her Life.

Her books were written at the order of her confessors, in plain Spanish, often in a hurry and with humor. Her Life, The Way of Perfection, The Book of the Foundations and The Interior Castle, which describes the soul as a castle of many rooms with God at its center, are still read as some of the best writing on prayer.

She died at Alba de Tormes on the night of 4 October 1582, the night Spain changed to the new calendar, so the next day was 15 October. She was canonized in 1622 and in 1970 became the first woman named a Doctor of the Church.
patronage: those who suffer headaches and illness
why_here: Teresa said prayer is nothing other than a close sharing between friends, taking time often to be alone with the one we know loves us. That is a definition a teenager can understand. The Prep's students are taught theology by monks and see the monks go to choir several times a day. Teresa is a good guide for the step from watching others pray to praying oneself.

She was also a woman of great practical sense, who ran houses, managed money and wrote letters to bankers and bishops. For the young women at the Prep she shows that holiness and competence go together. Her humor and her honesty about her own twenty years of half-hearted prayer are an encouragement to anyone who has tried and not got far.
relic: One small theca on the large board covered in grey linen, labelled "S. Theres. a Iesu" (St. Teresa of Jesus), its end hidden by the frame.
check: The paraphrase of her definition of prayer is from Life, chapter 8. Her patronage of Spain was argued in the 17th century and is not a single papal act.

name: St. Thomas Aquinas
title: Dominican priest, theologian, Doctor of the Church
summary: Thomas Aquinas was a Dominican priest and theologian, raised as a boy by the Benedictines of Monte Cassino, who wrote the Summa Theologiae and the hymns for Corpus Christi. Leo XIII named him patron of Catholic schools in 1880, and he is also a patron of students. He is the name saint of Br. Thomas, the abbey's librarian, and a patron of the Prep itself.
life: Thomas was born around 1225 at Roccasecca, the castle of the counts of Aquino, between Rome and Naples. When he was about five his parents gave him as an oblate to the Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, the monastery St. Benedict himself had founded, a few miles from home. They expected that one day he would be its abbot. He learned his letters, his psalms and his first theology from the monks, until war between the emperor and the pope drove him out around 1239 and he went to study at Naples.

At Naples he met the Dominicans, a new order of preaching friars who lived by begging, and in 1244 he joined them. His family was horrified. His brothers seized him on the road and kept him shut up in the family castle for about a year, and tried every means to change his mind. He did not change it, and in the end they let him go.

He studied under St. Albert the Great in Paris and Cologne. Large, quiet and slow to speak, he was nicknamed "the dumb ox" by fellow students. Albert is said to have answered that this ox would one day bellow so loud the whole world would hear. Thomas went on to teach at Paris, Naples and other cities, wrote commentaries on Scripture and on Aristotle, and above all the Summa Theologiae, a vast, orderly work meant for beginners in theology. He also wrote the hymns for the feast of Corpus Christi, including the Pange lingua and Tantum ergo.

On 6 December 1273, after something he experienced at Mass, he stopped writing. He told his secretary that all he had written seemed to him like straw compared with what he had seen. The Summa was never finished. Called to the Council of Lyon, he fell ill on the road and was taken to the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova, where he died on 7 March 1274.

He was canonized in 1323 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1567. His feast, 28 January, is the day his relics were moved to Toulouse in 1369. Leo XIII urged Catholic schools to study him in 1879 and named him their patron in 1880.
patronage: Catholic schools, colleges and universities (Leo XIII, 1880)
why_here: Thomas is the name saint of Br. Thomas, the abbey's librarian, who also coaches the Prep's Scholars' Bowl team. Leo XIII made Thomas the patron of every Catholic school, so he is already the patron of St. Bernard Prep and of the monks who teach there. The school's aim, a love of learning and a life of virtue, was his whole life.

He belongs to the monks in another way. He was raised by Benedictines at Monte Cassino, learning to read and pray in a monastery school much like the one at St. Bernard. Students who find study hard can take heart from a boy who was called a dumb ox.
relic: One small theca on the large board covered in grey linen, labelled "s. Thom. Aq. C. D." (Confessor, Doctor).

name: St. Thomas of Cori
title: Franciscan friar and preacher
summary: Thomas of Cori was a shepherd boy from the hills south of Rome who became a Franciscan priest. At Bellegra, near Subiaco, he founded a house of strict poverty and prayer and preached in the villages, though for forty years he felt no comfort in prayer. Patron of Cori and Bellegra, he is a saint for the plain perseverance monastic life asks.
life: Francesco Antonio Placidi was born at Cori, in the hills south of Rome, on 4 June 1655. His parents died when he was about fourteen, and he looked after his younger sisters and kept the family's sheep. He learned to read and kept learning while minding the flock. Once his sisters were settled, in 1677, he joined the Franciscan friars of the Observance and took the name Thomas. He was ordained a priest in 1683.

His superiors sent him to Civitella, now called Bellegra, a village on a hilltop near Subiaco. There he founded a ritiro, a house where friars could live the Franciscan rule in strict poverty, silence and prayer, and he spent most of the rest of his life there. He wrote its rules, and the idea spread to other houses. From Bellegra he went down to the villages of the region to preach, hear confessions and teach the catechism, and the poor people of the hills knew him well.

Those who knew him said he was cheerful and gentle. His own writings and his confessors tell a harder story. For some forty years he felt no comfort in prayer at all, and kept praying and working anyway. He died at Bellegra on 11 January 1729, and people from the villages around came in crowds to his funeral.
The friary at Bellegra still keeps his body and his memory. The hill towns of Lazio, where he walked and preached, remember him as a local saint, a shepherd boy who became a shepherd of souls.

He was beatified in 1786 and canonized by John Paul II in 1999. The label in this reliquary still calls him "B.", Blessed, as it does the other Franciscans beside him, which dates it to the years between 1825 and 1839.
why_here: Bellegra is a few miles from Subiaco, where St. Benedict lived as a hermit in a cave before founding his monasteries. Thomas built at Bellegra what the Rule asks of monks, a house of stability, silence and work, with the door open to the poor of the region.

His long dryness in prayer is worth knowing about in a monastery. Monks pray the office several times a day for decades, and most days it is not felt. Thomas kept faith without consolation for forty years and is honored for it. He is a patron for the ordinary perseverance that monastic life asks, and for anyone at the school who prays and feels nothing.
relic: One relic in the Gothic gilt reliquary of Franciscan saints, with Sts. Francis, Angelo of Acri, Leonard of Port Maurice and Pacificus, labelled "B. Thomae a Cora" (Blessed Thomas of Cori).
check: The forty years of dryness and his birth date (4 June 1655) are from standard Franciscan accounts and could be checked, as could the crowds at his funeral and his body being kept at Bellegra.

name: The Uganda Martyrs, St. Charles Lwanga and St. Matthias Mulumba
title: Martyrs of Uganda
summary: The Uganda Martyrs were Catholic converts at the court of King Mwanga II, many of them teenage pages, killed in 1885–1886 for their faith. Charles Lwanga, head of the pages, protected the boys from the king and was burned at Namugongo. Patron of African Catholic youth, Charles is the name saint of Br. Charles and a model for all who care for boarders.
life: Catholic missionaries, the White Fathers, came to the kingdom of Buganda, in what is now Uganda, in 1879, a little after Anglican missionaries from England. King Mutesa I let both teach. Many young men at court were drawn to the faith, among them the royal pages, boys and young men who served the king in his household.

Mutesa's son Mwanga II became king in 1884. He was young, suspicious of the foreigners and their religion, and he made sexual demands on the pages. Those who had become Christians refused him. In November 1885 he had Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe, his chief steward and a Catholic who had rebuked him for these things and for the murder of the Anglican bishop James Hannington, beheaded. Charles Lwanga, who was baptized that same night, took Joseph's place as head of the pages. He taught the boys, kept them away from the king, and baptized several of them himself.

In May 1886 the king turned on the Christians of his court. The night before the pages were led away, Charles baptized some who were still catechumens, among them Kizito, a boy of about fourteen. They were marched to Namugongo, and on 3 June 1886 Charles and many others were burned to death there. Charles was burned apart from the rest, slowly. Christians remember that he told the executioner he was pouring water on him and that he should repent.

Matthias Mulumba Kalemba was an older man, about fifty, a chief and a judge who had looked for the truth through Islam and the Anglican teachers before he became a Catholic in 1882. Arrested in the same days, he was mutilated and left to die at the place of execution, and he died after several days of suffering, shortly before the burning at Namugongo.

Twenty-two Catholics were beatified in 1920 and canonized by Paul VI in 1964. Anglican martyrs died alongside them, and the two churches honor them together. Every 3 June huge crowds walk to Namugongo.
patronage: African Catholic youth and Catholic Action (St. Charles Lwanga, Pius XI, 1934)
why_here: St. Charles Lwanga is the name saint of Br. Charles, the abbey's procurator. Most of the Uganda Martyrs were teenagers, young men living away from home in a large household under adults. Charles Lwanga was the older one who looked after them, taught them, and stood between them and an abuser. The Prep is a boarding school for students the same age, and its monks and staff are charged with the same care.
These martyrs can be prayed to for the students' courage to say no, for the adults who must protect them, and for the Prep's students from abroad, who live like the pages far from their families.
relic: One small theca on the large board covered in grey linen, labelled "Ex ossibus BB. Mart. Ugandensium" with the names "Matthiae Mulumba" and "Caroli Lwanga". "BB." dates the label to 1920–1964.
check: Pius XI's 1934 act (sources give 22 June 1934) named Lwanga patron of the youth and Catholic Action of much of tropical Africa. The exact day Matthias Mulumba died (around 30 May 1886) and his age are given differently in different accounts. The words to the executioner are tradition.

name: St. Ursula
title: Virgin and martyr of Cologne
summary: Almost nothing about St. Ursula is history. A 4th- or 5th-century inscription in Cologne honors virgins martyred there, and the legend of a British princess and eleven thousand companions grew later. Patron of schoolgirls and young women, she lent her name to the Ursulines, the first order of women devoted to teaching girls, and so suits the young women at the Prep.
life: Almost nothing about St. Ursula is history, and it is best to say so first. What is certain is a stone. In the church of St. Ursula in Cologne there is a Latin inscription, from the 4th or 5th century, in which a man named Clematius says he rebuilt, on that spot, a church in honor of holy virgins who had been martyred there. It gives no names and no number.

Out of that the legend grew. By the 10th century the martyrs had a leader, Ursula, and a number, eleven thousand. The number may come from a misreading of an abbreviation such as "XI M V", meant as eleven martyred virgins and read as eleven thousand. In its full medieval form, told in The Golden Legend, Ursula is a Christian princess of Britain promised to a pagan prince. She asks for three years' delay and sets out on pilgrimage to Rome with eleven thousand maidens. On the way back, at Cologne, they are all killed by the Huns, and Ursula is shot with an arrow when she refuses to marry their chief. None of this can be trusted as history.

In 1106 a large Roman burial ground was uncovered near the church in Cologne. Its bones, of men, women and children, were taken as the bones of Ursula and her companions and were sent out across Europe as relics. That is why so many churches, and this abbey, have them. Whose bones they really are cannot be known.

Her cult was strong for centuries. Hans Memling painted her story on a shrine in Bruges, and in 1535 St. Angela Merici founded at Brescia a company of women, the Ursulines, under her patronage, which became the first order of women in the Church devoted to teaching girls. Because so little is certain, her feast was removed from the General Roman Calendar in 1969, though it is still kept in many places.
why_here: Most of what the Prep's students know about Ursula, they would learn here, and it is a good lesson in itself. A saint's feast can be real devotion built on very little history, and the Church can be honest about that without mocking it.

Her best gift to schools came through the Ursulines, who took her name and taught girls in Europe and later in America, including New Orleans from 1727. St. Bernard Prep teaches young women as well as young men, and Ursula, through the women who borrowed her name, is a patron for the girls at the school and for the teachers, lay and monastic, who teach them.
relic: Two relics: one in the large oval in the velvet case studded with silver beads, labelled "s. Ursulae V.", and one on the large board covered in grey linen, labelled "Ex Os. S. Ursulae V. M."
check: The 1106 date of the Cologne discovery and the Ursulines in New Orleans from 1727 are from general knowledge and could be checked.

name: St. Valentine
title: Martyr
summary: Very little is known about St. Valentine, a Roman martyr of the 3rd century, perhaps the same man as a bishop of Terni. The stories linking him to romance are legends, and the custom of valentines began with medieval poets. Patron of engaged and married couples, he is a saint the monks can ask to keep the Prep's families strong.
life: Very little is known about St. Valentine, and what is known does not touch romance at all. Old Roman lists of martyrs name two men called Valentine on 14 February. One is a priest of Rome, martyred under the emperor Claudius II Gothicus around 269 and buried on the Via Flaminia north of the city. The other is a bishop of Terni, about sixty miles to the north, also martyred and also buried on the Via Flaminia. Many scholars think the two are one man, remembered in two places. Pope Julius I is said to have built a church over the grave in Rome in the 4th century.

The stories told about him come later and are legends. In one, he cured the blind daughter of his jailer and wrote her a farewell note signed "from your Valentine". In another, he secretly married soldiers whom the emperor had forbidden to marry. Neither has any support in ancient sources.

The link with love begins in the late Middle Ages, in England and France. Around 1380 Geoffrey Chaucer wrote in The Parliament of Fowls that birds choose their mates on St. Valentine's Day, and from courtly poetry the custom of sending valentines grew. It says more about spring than about the saint. Over the centuries Valentine also became, in parts of Germany and Austria, a saint prayed to against epilepsy, perhaps partly because his name sounds like the German word for falling.

Because so little is certain, his feast was dropped from the General Roman Calendar in 1969, though he remains in the Roman Martyrology. Relics said to be his are kept in a number of churches, in Rome, Terni, Dublin and elsewhere. The label here, "s. Valen. M", most likely means Valentine, Martyr.
why_here: The Prep's families rest on marriages, and many parents carry the work of supporting a son or daughter at a boarding school. The monks can ask St. Valentine, whatever is known of him, to keep those marriages strong.

There is also something for the students. Every February the world sells them a feast that has nothing to do with the man. A Catholic school can tell the truth, that Valentine was a martyr who died for Christ and whose story is mostly lost, and still bless what the day has come to mean, faithful love between a man and a woman.
relic: One small theca on the large board covered in grey linen, labelled "s. Valen. M" (likely Valentine, Martyr).
check: The reading "Valen." as Valentine is likely, not certain. The date around 269 and the church of Julius I are tradition from the old martyr lists and could be checked.

name: St. Valerius of Trier
title: Second bishop of Trier
summary: Valerius is honored as the second bishop of Trier, though almost nothing about him is certain beyond his name and his place in the list. The legend that St. Peter sent him cannot be proved, but his tomb is still venerated at the Benedictine abbey of St. Matthias. Patron of Trier, his relic is a sign of the abbey's German roots.
life: Trier, on the Moselle in western Germany, is one of the oldest cities north of the Alps. In the late Roman empire it was an imperial capital, where Constantine lived for a time. Its church is very old too, and Trier's tradition names its first three bishops as Eucharius, Valerius and Maternus.

A medieval legend, written down in the 10th century, makes them disciples sent from Rome by St. Peter himself. In that story Maternus died on the way, and Peter gave the others his staff, with which they raised him to life. Eucharius then became the first bishop of Trier, Valerius the second and Maternus the third. Historians think the first bishops of Trier lived much later than Peter, more likely in the 3rd century, and that Valerius may have died in the early 4th. Almost nothing about his life is known for certain beyond his name and his place in the list.

What is certain is that he has been honored at Trier since early times. He and Eucharius were buried outside the city walls, in the cemetery where a church grew up over their tombs. A Benedictine abbey was founded there. In the 12th century relics of the apostle St. Matthias were found there too, and the abbey took his name. The Benedictine abbey of St. Matthias still stands, with monks living in it, and the tombs of Eucharius and Valerius are still venerated in its crypt. Trier keeps Valerius's feast on 29 January.

The story of the three bishops was told and retold at Trier because it claimed for the city a church founded by the apostles. That claim cannot be proved. But the graves are real, and generations of Christians at Trier, and of monks at St. Matthias, have prayed at them for some seventeen hundred years. Pilgrims still come to the abbey, the only place north of the Alps that claims the tomb of an apostle.
why_here: His relic has a twin, likely of St. Eucharius, in the same jewelled frame and the same red-ink hand. Along with a relic of the Martyrs of Trier and one from the Abbey of St. Matthias, it may have come to Cullman as one gift from Trier, perhaps from the monks of St. Matthias to the monks of St. Bernard.

That makes Valerius a sign of the abbey's German roots. The monks came by way of St. Vincent in Pennsylvania from Metten Abbey in Bavaria, and Cullman was settled by German immigrants. The monks can pray to him for their brothers in the old country and for the bond between Benedictine houses.
relic: One relic in a jewelled gilt reliquary, the twin of the one likely of St. Eucharius, labelled in red ink "S. Valerio".
check: That the relics came as one gift from St. Matthias in Trier is the catalogue's suggestion, not a known fact.

name: St. Vincent Ferrer
title: Dominican priest and preacher
summary: Vincent Ferrer was a Dominican preacher from Valencia who helped end the Great Western Schism and spent twenty years preaching repentance across Europe. His campaigns also put heavy pressure on the Jews of Spain, and that belongs to his story too. Patron of Valencia and of builders, he is a saint for the abbey's craftsman monks.
life: Vincent Ferrer was born at Valencia, in eastern Spain, on 23 January 1350, and entered the Dominican order there at seventeen. He studied and taught philosophy and theology, and by his thirties he was known as a scholar and a powerful preacher.

His life was bound up with the Great Western Schism, which began in 1378, when rival popes in Rome and Avignon each claimed the whole Church. Good and learned people stood on both sides. Vincent backed the Avignon line and served as confessor and adviser to Pedro de Luna, who became the Avignon pope Benedict XIII. When Benedict refused every way of ending the split, Vincent at last withdrew his support, in 1416. Since the kings of Spain followed him, this helped the Council of Constance end the schism with the election of Martin V in 1417.

From 1399 he spent his last twenty years on the road, on foot or on a donkey, preaching repentance through Spain, southern France, northern Italy and Switzerland. He preached that the last judgment was near, and he was sometimes called the Angel of the Apocalypse. Large crowds followed him from town to town, including bands of penitents who scourged themselves, and he organized them to keep them from disorder. Many miracles were told of him, and many who heard him changed their lives.

His campaigns also put heavy pressure on the Jews of Spain. He preached in synagogues, supported laws that pushed Jews into separate quarters, and took part in the forced debate at Tortosa in 1413–1414. Many Jews converted in those years, often under fear. That is part of his story too, and it should be told honestly.
He died at Vannes in Brittany on 5 April 1419 and is buried in its cathedral. He was canonized in 1455 by Pope Callixtus III, himself from Valencia.
why_here: The abbey has a long line of craftsman monks, builders and carvers among them, and Vincent is the traditional patron of builders, because he spent his life building up the Church. The monks who keep the buildings and build furniture and altars can count him as their own.

He also shows the students something worth learning. A saint can be holy and still be wrong on important things. Vincent helped heal a divided Church, and he also hurt the Jews of Spain. Studying him honestly is a lesson in charity and truth.
relic: One relic in a theca of its own, labelled "S. Vinc. Fer. C." (Confessor).
check: His patronage of builders and plumbers is traditional and the reason given for it is popular, not official. The penitents he organized and his role in the laws on Jewish quarters are summarized from general histories.
